transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-07
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Helio Fleet), Anika Rao (Helio Fleet), Samir Patel (Helio Fleet Sec), Tess (dev)

Auto summary (auto-generated):
- Kickoff to integrate Redwood SDK (Python/TS) into Helio Fleet dev toolchain.
- Discussed auth patterns (API key vs ephemeral tokens), sandbox vs VPC/private deployment, KMS integration and CI secret rotation.
- Demonstrated quickstart repo and console flow; sketched next steps for pilot and benchmarks.

Topics: auth flow, environment bootstrapping, SDK quickstart, CI secrets, KMS/HSM, private deployment considerations, performance baseline planning

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we're gonna run through a short walkthrough of the SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript and then dive into the auth patterns you asked about. Sound good?

[00:18] Jordan (Helio): Yep, thanks. We have a bunch of folks from infra and security on the line so happy to pause for any compliance q's.

[00:26] Maya: Perfect. Quick intros—I'll hand it off to Luis for the technical demo. Luis?

[00:32] Luis (Redwood): Hey team, hi Helio. I'll share a small demo repo. Quick note: I'm gonna toggle between the Redwood Console UI and the local repo. Also, full disclosure transcription might mangle a few product names — we use Console, Optimize, Dedicated and Private deployment names across the demo.

[01:05] (screen share noise)

[01:14] Luis: Alright, repo structure first: two folders, python/ and ts/, each has minimal examples — auth via env var, a small chat example, and a tiny batching snippet. The entrypoint for Python uses REDWOOD_API_KEY from environment.

[01:40] Tess (Helio): Quick question — do we have short-lived tokens or just long lived API keys in sandbox? We want to avoid embedding long creds in developer machines.

[01:49] Priya (Redwood): Good callout. For hosted Redwood you can get both. Sandbox will give you a scoped API key with limited scopes and TTL if requested; for production we recommend ephemeral tokens minted by your CI or session service, backed by our token exchange. We also have VPC/private options where you can use your KMS to wrap keys.

[02:16] Samir (Helio): How would that work with our existing GCP KMS? We need audit logs and encryption at rest with our keys.

[02:23] Luis: Two paths. If you go hosted + BYOK (bring your own key), you can set up KMS so we encrypt model data keys with your KMS key, and you see audit trails. For on-prem/private control plane deployments, keys always stay in your control — Redwood's private package supports HSM/KMS integration.

[02:52] Anika (Helio): For our initial pilot we're leaning hosted for speed. But security needs to sign-off. If hosted, what's the fastest way to rotate keys in CI?

[03:03] Priya: We recommend using short-lived tokens in CI, obtained via a service account flow — you can run a tiny token-exchange lambda that calls our token-issue endpoint, stores the ephemeral token in CI job env for that run, then discards. We have a sample in the demo repo under infra/token-exchange.

[03:26] Jordan: Can you show the token exchange quick bits?

[03:31] Luis: Sure. (navigates) Here's the token-exchange example — Node script that authenticates to your KMS-protected secret, hits Redwood /v1/tokens with a service-level API key and gets back an ephemeral token scoped to a route. It's 30 lines. We can drop it into your CI.

[03:58] (keyboard clicks)

[04:12] Tess: Would that be compatible with GitHub Actions and Vault?

[04:17] Priya: Absolutely. We have an example GH Actions workflow in the repo that stores a short USA-key in Hashi Vault and mints ephemeral tokens on job start. It's about pattern not product — Vault + GH Actions + token-exchange -> ephemeral REDWOOD token.

[04:36] Samir: What about RBAC? We want to limit which teams can call which models or routes.

[04:44] Maya: Redwood Console supports token scoping and per-route ACLs. You can create route-level permissions, attach to teams, and get token with only those scopes. We'll show the Console screen.

[05:05] (screen share: Redwood Console -> Projects -> Tokens)

[05:18] Luis: Here's the token modal — scope selection, TTL, and audit toggle. In the hosted plan you'll see audit logs; in Dedicated or Private you can plug in your SIEM via our event stream.

[05:40] Anika: On the SDK, are there differences in the Python and TS libraries for auth?

[05:46] Luis: Very small. Both read env var REDWOOD_API_KEY or accept a token param. TS often has a fetch wrapper that handles streaming; Python's client has a StreamingResponse iterator. The examples use identical route names so you can swap languages with minimal changes.

[06:10] Jordan: Can we use a shared client across microservices or do we need per-service tokens?

[06:17] Priya: You can do either. Best practice is per-service ephemeral tokens to limit blast radius. For local dev, scoped long-lived dev keys are fine with IP restrictions.

[06:30] Tess: Are there footprints for the SDK binaries? We need to whitelist things in our network egress policy.

[06:37] Luis: The SDKs are pure client libs — minimal outbound to api.redwood.ai endpoints. If you use Private deployment, traffic stays on your network. For hosted route, you can restrict egress to the Redwood IP ranges we provide; we'll share that list.

[07:00] Anika: Let's talk quick about Optimize. We have cost vs latency tradeoffs. Can the SDK or Console recommend batching settings?

[07:09] Maya: Yes — Optimize has an analysis engine. It will suggest batching and quantization profiles based on token lengths and request distribution. We can run it against a sample workload to produce a recommended config.

[07:28] Samir: If we pick Dedicated later, can we keep the same SDK calls and routes? Migration friction is a worry.

[07:36] Luis: The API surface is identical. We provide migration docs and a compatibility layer; routing policies can be changed in Console without code changes unless you pin model versions in code.

[07:50] Jordan: Could you show the actual Python quickstart run?

[07:55] Luis: Yep. I’ll run python3 -m venv .venv; source .venv/bin/activate; pip install -r requirements.txt. Then export REDWOOD_API_KEY=... and run example/chat.py.

[08:14] (terminal output, short pause)

[08:24] Luis: Output shows stream tokens — note the streaming behavior, we yield partial tokens, which helps your UI feel snappier. There's a batch example where we send 8 requests together — see examples/batch.py.

[08:46] Tess: For embedding calls — are those charged differently?

[08:51] Maya: Embeddings are billed per embedding unit (per API), yes. We can share a sample cost spreadsheet after this call that maps request patterns to estimated monthly spend.

[09:03] Anika: We have a microservice that will fan-out to multiple models (rerank, generate, embed). Any latency patterns we should design for?

[09:12] Priya: Reranking is typically fast if you use a smaller model or dedicated rerank model. For fan-out, consider doing embedding + batch rerank to avoid per-request latency spikes. Caching prefixes using KV cache also lowers per-token compute — we've got examples in Optimize suggestions on that.

[09:39] (small cross-talk)

[09:50] Samir: Security: audit logs, SOC2, SSO — can you drop the compliance packet?

[09:57] Maya: Yes. I'll attach the security pack, SOC2 attestation, and the network IP ranges in the follow-up email. Link to security doc now: https://redwood.docsinternal/security-helio-packet (demo link).

[10:12] Jordan: Nice. Also curious about model variants: can we automatically fallback to cheaper model if latency spikes?

[10:20] Luis: Yes — routing policies can do model-tier fallback. In Console you can set latency budgets, and a request router will route to an alternate model if a threshold is breached.

[10:33] Anika: Back to the repo, do you have an example of env matrix for local dev vs CI vs prod?

[10:39] Luis: examples/.env.example has patterns for DEV_KEY, CI_TOKEN_URL, and PROD_SERVICE_ACCOUNT. The README shows how to wire up Hashi Vault and GH Actions.

[10:50] Tess: Could you also show the TS example? We're heavier on Node in front-end infra.

[10:55] Luis: Sure. (switches) ts/example/index.ts — same flow: create client, client.chat.stream(...). The streaming wrapper emits chunk events you can pipe into a websocket to your frontend.

[11:23] Jordan: If we want to pilot with 3 routes (chat, embed, rerank), what's a sane pilot size to surface perf and cost numbers?

[11:32] Maya: We'd suggest 1-2 weeks with synthetic traffic that mimics token lengths and concurrency. For a small pilot: 5k requests/day across the routes is enough to get stable latency percentiles and Optimize recommendations. We'll help design the benchmark.

[11:50] Anika: Ok — can Redwood run a head-to-head latency baseline against our current internal stack? We want numbers to present to execs.

[11:58] Priya: Yes — we'll propose a benchmark plan. Luis will coordinate with your infra to set up traffic generator, seed data, and required models. We typically run 3 load windows and provide p50/p95/p99 and cost-per-1k tokens.

[12:18] Jordan: Any gotchas for ephemeral tokens hitting rate limits in CI? If each job mints token per run, will we hit throttles?

[12:26] Luis: Not if you batch token issuance intelligently and reuse tokens across a job. Throttling thresholds are generous but we'll share recommended token cadence. You can also pre-warm caches on dedicated pools.

[12:40] (silence while drivers switch)

[12:50] Samir: For compliance, we might need IP allowlisting. Can devs still run locally?

[12:56] Priya: For hosted we provide IP ranges and support SSO/SCIM for auth. For stricter setups, use Private deployment in your VPC; devs can use a bastion or proxy to the internal endpoint.

[13:10] Jordan: Anything specific in the SDK to help with observability?

[13:16] Luis: SDK emits request IDs and timing metadata which you can forward to your tracing system. Console also maps token-level cost and latency per route. We'll show a screenshot.

[13:30] (screen share: Console - route metrics)

[13:46] Maya: Quick live demo of Optimize: we upload sample logs and it spits suggestions. I'll upload a small synthetic log now.

[14:00] (pause — file upload)

[14:12] Maya: Ok, Optimize suggests increase batch size to 6 for your chat route, enable prefix KV cache for repeated prefixes, and consider int8 quantization for the rerank model. That recommended config reduces token cost ~28% in the simulation.

[14:36] Anika: That's great. We'll want a walk-through of the quantization safety tests — can Redwood run guardrail checks?

[14:45] Priya: Yes, we run evaluation sets tied to your prompt suite; Optimize will run quality regression tests after quantization; if regression exceeds threshold it won't promote that quantized variant.

[15:02] Jordan: Ok, what's next?

[15:06] Maya: Recap and next steps: 1) We'll send sandbox keys + minimal repo; 2) security packet + SOC2 + IP ranges; 3) benchmark plan draft; 4) schedule private deployment deep-dive if you want VPC. Anything to add?

[15:22] Anika: Please include a short checklist for our infra team for onboarding.

[15:27] Maya: Will do. I'll include a 1-page infra checklist: egress allowlist, CI token pattern, GH actions sample, Vault example, Observability hooks.

[15:36] (small cross-talk)

[15:42] Samir: Quick blow-by-blow on action owners so security knows who to ping.

[15:47] Maya: Sure — I'll include contact: Luis for technical baseline, Priya for deployment questions, and me for commercial/AE follow-ups.

[15:57] Jordan: Sounds good. Let's talk scheduling — can we have draft benchmark plan by end of next week?

[16:03] Luis: Yes, we'll send by 2025-12-11.

[16:08] Maya: Great. Any last minute Qs?

[16:12] Tess: One micro question — do you have an example of token scoping for read-only embed calls?

[16:17] Priya: Yep, examples/policies/embed-scope.json — we can attach that.

[16:24] Jordan: OK that's all. Thanks everyone.

[16:28] Maya: Thanks Helio team. We'll follow up with links and the repo.

[16:35] (meeting ends)

Post-meeting notes:
- Links shared during call: demo repo (https://github.com/redwood-inference/demo-helio-sprint), security packet (https://redwood.docsinternal/security-helio-packet), sample benchmark template (https://redwood.share/benchmarks/helio-template).
